- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

content.text: The candidate designs array was empty (`[]`) — no designs were transmitted. I verified the reference target and the ground truth for the test case, then judged the archetype space that any candidate must fall into, so the parent still gets an actionable fidelity verdict.

ranking.approach_name: (NO CANDIDATES SUPPLIED — archetype A) Snap-rounded planar arrangement + half-edge face labelling
(archetype B) Vatti/Clipper2-style scanline clone: local minima, active edge list, scanbeams, windCnt/windCnt2, OutRec rings + joins
(archetype C) Martinez-Rueda / Bentley-Ottmann sweep with inOut/otherInOut event annotation and result-edge chaining
(archetype D) Trapezoidal / vertical-slab decomposition, per-slab fill test, then merge cells and re-extract contours
(archetype E) Rasterize on unit grid + marching squares / contour trace as the production engine
(archetype F) Greiner-Hormann / Weiler-Atherton vertex-list clipping, applied pairwise

input.best_approach: Snap-rounded planar arrangement with half-edge face labelling: (1) collect all subject and clip edges tagged by operand set; (2) compute all pairwise segment intersections with exact i128 rational arithmetic and round to the integer grid via Hobby hot-pixel routing (every segment passing through a hot pixel is re-routed through its center), with a provable termination bound; (3) build a planar subdivision of the snapped, non-crossing segment set (twin half-edges, vertices sorted by angle with exact i128 cross/dot comparators, coincident collinear overlaps merged into one edge carrying two winding deltas); (4) label every face with a PAIR of winding numbers (w_subject, w_clip) by BFS propagation across the dual graph from the unbounded face, adding the crossed edge's directional delta; (5) evaluate inside_subj = fill(w_subject) and inside_clip = fill(w_clip) SEPARATELY under the single FillRule (EvenOdd: odd; NonZero: !=0; Positive: >0; Negative: <0), then combine per ClipType (Intersection: both; Union: either; Difference: subj && !clip; Xor: subj != clip); (6) keep only half-edges whose incident face is selected and whose twin's face is not, and extract boundary cycles by "next half-edge = most-clockwise turn at the destination vertex", which automatically splits pinch vertices into separate contours; (7) cleanup with exact i128: drop duplicate points, iteratively remove collinear vertices until a fixed point, drop cycles with <3 points or exactly zero signed area; (8) normalize orientation so outer contours have positive signed area and holes negative, independent of input orientation, and emit outers and holes flat in one Paths64.
input.rationale:
NOTE FIRST: the candidate design list I was given was literally `[]`, so there was nothing to score. Rather than return nothing, I established the fidelity ground truth and ranked the six archetypes any candidate must instantiate, through the fidelity lens only.

Ground truth I pinned down for the test (A = [0,100]^2 CCW, B = [50,150]^2 CCW, FillRule::EvenOdd), which is the yardstick every design must be measured against: Intersect -> 1 path, the square (50,50),(100,50),(100,100),(50,100), signed area +2500. Union -> 1 path, 8 vertices, +17500. Difference -> 1 path, 6 vertices, +7500. Xor -> 2 SEPARATE paths of 6 vertices each, +7500 apiece, because the two L-lobes meet only at the isolated points (100,50) and (50,100). Area identity: 17500 + 2500 == 10000 + 10000. The reference binary prints "1\n" with or without argv, confirmed by running it.

Fidelity discrimination is decided by three tests, not by the printed `1` (every archetype except the rasterizer prints 1 for Intersect, so the smoke test is nearly information-free): (i) does Xor return 2 paths rather than one self-touching ring; (ii) is the fill rule applied per operand set, so that two coincident squares BOTH in `subjects` under EvenOdd cancel and an annulus test yields outer+hole = 2 paths; (iii) is orientation normalized so reversing both inputs to CW still yields positive-area outers.

The arrangement approach wins because each fidelity requirement maps onto an explicit, inspectable step: the (w_subj, w_clip) face label IS Clipper2's windCnt/windCnt2 semantics stated declaratively; most-clockwise-turn cycle extraction IS the pinch-splitting rule; signed area IS the hole convention. It is also the only archetype where hole/outer classification needs no ray casting and no nesting heuristics. Vatti scores a perfect 10 on fidelity in principle — it is Clipper2's own algorithm family — but that score is unreachable in practice: a from-scratch clone of scanbeam horizontal-edge processing and join resolution, black-box, with no source to check against, has a high probability of subtly-wrong output ring counts and of non-terminating horizontal loops, and its failures are opaque (you cannot localize a wrong path count to a step). Fidelity you cannot land is worth less than 9-out-of-10 fidelity you can verify, so I rank the arrangement above it. Martinez-Rueda is a reasonable third but its classic inOut/otherInOut formulation encodes even-odd-only "insideness" for two simple operands; generalizing it to four fill rules and to self-intersecting multi-contour operand sets means reintroducing winding counters anyway, at which point you have a less structured version of the arrangement. Rasterization and Greiner-Hormann are disqualifying, not merely weak: i64 coordinates make a unit grid impossible, and GH cannot survive collinear overlap or vertex-on-edge, both of which occur in this very test set.
ideas_to_graft: From Vatti/Clipper2: carry TWO winding counters per edge (own-set and other-set) rather than a single merged winding. This is the single most important fidelity idea; it is what makes EvenOdd mean 'parity within subjects' and 'parity within clips' independently, and it is required for Difference/Xor to be asymmetric in the right way.

From Vatti/Clipper2: represent output as doubly-linked point rings with an explicit owner/parent pointer per ring, so hole-vs-outer is a structural fact (nesting depth) that can be cross-checked against the signed-area sign. Disagreement between the two is a cheap always-on assertion that catches topology bugs the area test alone would miss.

From Martinez-Rueda: explicit classification of coincident collinear overlapping edges into same-transition vs opposite-transition, and collapsing them to a single arrangement edge that carries the SUM of winding deltas. Without this, two polygons sharing an edge exactly (very common, and present implicitly in the test set) produce duplicated boundary edges and spurious zero-width contours.

From Martinez-Rueda: sweep-order event processing as an O((n+k) log n) way to find intersections, usable as the intersection-enumeration front end of the arrangement instead of an O(n^2) pairwise scan, without changing any semantics.

From snap-rounding literature (Hobby / iterated snap rounding): make grid rounding a bounded, monotone procedure - round intersections to hot-pixel centers, then re-route every segment crossing a hot pixel through that center, and prove/assert a strictly decreasing count of off-grid crossings plus an invariant that no coordinate ever leaves the input bounding box. Also hard-cap the iteration count with a deterministic tie-break fallback so the engine can never hang.

From the trapezoidal/slab archetype: vertical-slab evaluation is an excellent independent ORACLE. Decompose by all distinct x of vertices and intersections, evaluate the fill predicate on each trapezoid exactly with i128 rationals, and sum areas. This gives an exact expected total area to compare against the engine output with zero shared code - far stronger than sampled point-in-polygon.

From the rasterization archetype: keep it, but only as a small-coordinate differential oracle (coords bounded to roughly [-64, 64], sample cell centers at half-integer offsets to avoid boundary ties, compare per-cell inside/outside against the engine's output contours). Never as the engine.

Verification harness ideas worth stealing regardless of engine: canonicalize each output path (rotate to lexicographically smallest vertex, preserve direction) so path-set comparison is rotation-insensitive but orientation-sensitive; assert the four algebraic identities with exact i128 areas; assert idempotence (Union(X,X)==Union(X,{})), commutativity of Union/Intersect/Xor, and that Difference(A,B) union Intersect(A,B) reproduces A; assert every returned path has >=3 points, nonzero area, no duplicate consecutive points, and no collinear triple.
fatal_flaws: Single merged winding number over all subject+clip edges instead of a per-operand-set pair. This is the most dangerous flaw because it still prints `1` for the required test and still satisfies the area identities on single-contour inputs, so it looks correct while being semantically wrong: two coincident squares in `subjects` under EvenOdd must cancel (Union -> annulus, 2 paths), and a merged winding gives 1 path. Any design that says 'accumulate winding, then apply the fill rule' without saying 'twice, once per set' is broken.

Emitting self-touching single contours instead of splitting at pinch vertices. Directly wrong on this exact test set: Xor of the two squares must be 2 paths meeting at (100,50) and (50,100). Cycle extraction must use most-clockwise-turn at each vertex, angularly sorted, so a degree-4 pinch vertex is traversed as two independent cycles. A naive 'follow the next unused edge' walk yields 1 path with a wrong vertex count.

Preserving input orientation instead of normalizing it. Clipper2 returns outers positive and holes negative regardless of how the inputs were wound; a design that copies input orientation returns negative-area outers for CW input, which then makes area-sign-based hole classification and every area identity check silently sign-flipped.

f64 arithmetic for orientation/intersection predicates. With i64 coordinates near +/-9e18, a 53-bit mantissa loses the sign of the cross product entirely, which changes TOPOLOGY (edge ordering at a vertex, above/below in a sweep) and therefore the number of output contours. All predicates must be exact i128 (cross products of i64 differences fit in i128; segment-intersection comparisons need rational comparison via cross-multiplication, also i128, with overflow-conscious ordering).

Unbounded 'recompute intersections until nothing new appears' rounding loops with no monotone measure. Rounding an intersection onto the grid can create a new crossing, whose rounding creates another; without a hot-pixel argument and an explicit decreasing quantity plus an iteration cap, this is a genuine non-termination hazard on adversarial integer inputs, and it is the most likely way a design hangs rather than merely returns wrong results.

Collinear-vertex removal performed BEFORE topology extraction. A vertex that looks collinear on its own contour may be the pinch/split point where two output contours meet, or the point where a hole touches its outer; deleting it early merges contours and changes the returned path count. Cleanup must run strictly after cycle extraction.

Non-iterated collinear cleanup. Removing collinear triples in a single forward pass leaves new collinear triples created by earlier removals (classic case: two unit squares sharing an edge, Union must return a 4-vertex rectangle, a single pass returns 6 vertices). Must loop to a fixed point, and must re-check the wrap-around neighbours of the first/last vertices.

Not discarding exactly-zero-area and sub-3-point contours, or testing them in floating point. Spike contours (A,B,A) and slivers created by rounding have exact zero area and must be dropped; Intersect of two squares touching only along an edge or at a corner must return 0 paths, not a degenerate 1. Zero-area detection must be exact integer accumulation, and dropping a degenerate ring can expose further collinear vertices, so cleanup and degeneracy-dropping must be mutually iterated.

Treating the operand SETS as pairwise operations: doing Difference(subject_i, clip_j) for each pair and concatenating. Clipper2 resolves the whole subject set under the fill rule and the whole clip set under the fill rule, then combines once; pairwise-and-concatenate produces overlapping duplicate contours and an inflated path count.

Greiner-Hormann / Weiler-Atherton vertex-list clipping in any form. It has no representation for collinear overlap or for an intersection that coincides with a vertex - both present in the test configuration - and its degenerate cases classically either drop a contour or loop forever chasing an entry/exit flag that never flips. It also offers no route to NonZero/Positive/Negative.

Rasterization/marching-squares as the production engine. Infeasible at i64 range (a 1-unit grid over 1.8e19 units), and even where feasible it returns staircase contours: vertex counts and coordinates would not match Clipper2 on anything not axis-aligned. Fine as a bounded oracle, disqualifying as the engine.

Hole classification by ray-casting against the OUTPUT contours while ignoring boundary-touching cases. A hole whose boundary touches its outer at a single point (or along a segment) puts the ray through a vertex/edge, and a ray caster without a consistent 'count only upward crossings, half-open at the lower endpoint' rule misclassifies it, flipping its sign and corrupting both the path set and every area identity.

Any design whose only stated acceptance criterion is that the program prints `1`. That value is produced by nearly every archetype including badly broken ones; a design that does not commit to the Xor-returns-2-paths, EvenOdd-annulus, and orientation-normalization checks has no fidelity evidence at all.
